content: Cinchonism, also known as quinism, is a pathological condition in humans that arises from an overdose of quinine or its natural source, cinchona bark. Quinine is a medication used to treat resistant malaria and nocturnal muscle cramps, and it can also function as an abortifacient. In much smaller quantities, quinine is included in tonic drinks as a bittering agent. Cinchonism can develop from therapeutic doses of quinine, either from a single large dose, multiple large doses, or prolonged use of small doses over time. However, it does not typically occur from the small amounts of quinine found in tonic drinks, unless tonic water is consumed in excessive quantities over an extended period. Additionally, quinidine, a Class 1A anti-arrhythmic drug, can also induce cinchonism. Mild cinchonism, which may result from standard therapeutic doses of quinine, is characterized by symptoms such as flushed and sweaty skin, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), blurred vision, impaired hearing, confusion, reversible high-frequency hearing loss, headache, abdominal pain, rashes, lichen-like photosensitivity, vertigo, dizziness, dysphoria (a sense of unease), nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. In cases of large quinine doses, severe symptoms of cinchonism may occur. These include skin rashes, deafness, somnolence, reduced visual acuity or blindness, anaphylactic shock, cardiac rhythm or conduction disturbances, and death due to cardiotoxicity. Quinine overdose can also lead to a rare hypersensitivity reaction known as blackwater fever, which is characterized by massive hemolysis, hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and renal failure. Patients treated with quinine may also experience hypoglycemia, particularly when the drug is administered intravenously, and hypotension (low blood pressure). In very high doses, exceeding those used for malaria treatment, quinine administered during the first trimester of pregnancy may act as an abortifacient or cause birth defects, most notably deafness. Most symptoms of cinchonism, except in severe cases, are reversible and resolve once quinine is discontinued.
